name: (You Gotta) Fight for Your Right (To Party!)

podcast.body: Often regarded as a "frat boy novelty song," especially after its video release, this track was also a fusion of rock with big guitars and heavy drums, featuring rapping instead of singing. Adam Yauch and a friend named Tom wrote the song as a parody of contemporary rock anthems like Twisted Sister's "I Wanna Rock" and Quiet Riot's "Bang Your Head," though this satirical intent was largely "lost on 95% of the people who heard it." The music video, featuring cameos from LL Cool J, Rick Rubin, and MTV's Tabitha Soren, had an almost nonexistent budget, with all the whipped cream used for pies scrounged from dumpsters behind supermarkets, described as "sour and rancid and smelled awful." "This was supposed to be a parody of those types of songs, but that was lost on 95% of the people who heard it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song is mentioned as an example of the "frat boy stuff" from the Beastie Boys' first album, which disappointed fans who were expecting more of the same when *Paul's Boutique* was released. "Everyone who was hoping for more songs like Fight for Your Right to Party and Girls, and all the other frat boy stuff from the first album was very disappointed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song was widely perceived as a "fratboy novelty song," particularly after its video release, which featured cameos from LL Cool J, Rick Rubin, and MTV's Tabitha Soren, and used rancid, dumpster-scrounged whipped cream due to a low budget. Written by Adam Yauch and his friend Tom, it was intended as a parody of rock anthems like Twisted Sister's "I Wanna Rock" and Quiet Riot's "Cum On Feel the Noize," but 95% of its audience missed the satirical intent. Musically, it distinguished itself by featuring big guitars and heavy drums alongside rapping instead of singing. "You gotta fight! For your right! To party!"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
